summary: Philipp Schmid of Google DeepMind contrasts traditional software development—spec, code, tests, deploy—with the iterative agent loop of defining instructions, running, observing, and adjusting prompts or tools. He uses the metaphor of a traffic controller (traditional software, where you control exact steps) versus a dispatcher (agents, where you define the goal but not the path). He then presents five key differences. First, text is the new state: instead of Boolean flags and structured data, agents rely on semantic meaning in text, enabling richer user interactions like approving a research plan while adding constraints in natural language. Second, hand over control: deterministic workflows (e.g., a fixed subscription-cancellation flow) cannot anticipate dynamic intent shifts; agents must react to changing context. Third, errors are inputs, not restart triggers: unlike cheap HTTP retries, restarting a 15-minute agent wastes compute and loses context, so errors should be fed back to the model. Fourth, move from unit tests to evals: agents are non-deterministic, so the question is how often something works, not whether a fixed input always yields a fixed output; results are subjective and require LLM-as-judge or human evaluation. Fifth, agents evolve and APIs do not: endpoints like deleteItem feel self-explanatory to their developer, but an agent only sees the function schema and docstring, so tools must be self-documenting with semantic interfaces. Schmid summarizes: give trust but verify, stop forcing the model into rigid workflows, preserve meaning as context, design for recovery, evaluate rather than only assert, and build to delete because the bitter lesson means software is disposable and will be rebuilt with better models.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Traditional software is like a traffic controller controlling exact steps; agents are like a dispatcher defining the goal but not the path.
Text replaces structured state—agents understand semantic meaning, enabling richer interactions than Boolean flags and data structures.
Hand over control: deterministic workflows cannot model dynamic intent shifts, so engineers must trust the LLM in non-deterministic environments.
Errors are inputs, not restart triggers—restarting a long-running agent wastes compute and loses context; feed errors back to the model instead.
Evals replace unit tests—the right question is how often the agent works, not whether a fixed input always yields a fixed output; results are subjective.
Senior engineers struggle because they carry implicit context that agents lack; tools must be self-documenting with semantic interfaces, not assume years of developer expertise.
Build to delete: software is disposable and will be rebuilt many times with better models and better agents.
Give trust but verify: stop fighting the model by forcing it into rigid step-by-step workflows.
Design for recovery: agents are not perfect, especially long-running ones, so systems must handle unexpected behavior gracefully.
Understand the five key differences between building traditional software and building AI agents

sections.title: Introduction: Traditional Software vs Agents
sections.summary: Schmid introduces himself and his work on agents at Google DeepMind. He contrasts traditional software development (spec, code, tests, deploy) with the iterative agent loop (define instructions, run, observe, adjust prompts/tools, repeat). He uses the metaphor of a traffic controller versus a dispatcher: in traditional software you control exact steps, while with agents you define the goal but not the path.

sections.title: Text Is the New State
sections.summary: First shift: text replaces structured state. Instead of Boolean flags and data structures, agents understand semantic meaning. Examples include approving a deep research plan while adding natural-language constraints, and dynamic user preferences like switching between Celsius and Fahrenheit for cooking that fixed flags cannot capture.

sections.title: Hand Over Control
sections.summary: Second shift: hand over control. Deterministic workflows like fixed subscription-cancellation flows cannot model dynamic intent shifts where a user changes their mind mid-conversation. Engineers must trust the LLM to react dynamically rather than forcing purely deterministic stateful workflows.

sections.title: Errors Are Just Inputs
sections.summary: Third shift: treat errors as inputs, not restart triggers. Drawing an analogy to Go's error handling, Schmid argues that restarting a 5-to-15-minute agent wastes compute and loses context. Errors should be fed back to the model with workarounds to keep the flow moving forward.

sections.title: From Unit Tests to Evals
sections.summary: Fourth shift: replace unit tests with evals. Agents are non-deterministic, so the question is how often something works, not whether a fixed input always yields a fixed output. Results are subjective, requiring LLM-as-judge or human expert evaluation. Engineers should trace agent behavior but measure success on outcomes, not exact steps.

sections.title: Agents Evolve and APIs Don't
sections.summary: Fifth shift: APIs must become agent-ready. A deleteItem endpoint feels self-explanatory to its developer, but an agent only sees the function schema and docstring, lacking years of implicit context. Tools must be self-documenting with semantic interfaces, written for agents, not assuming developer expertise.

sections.title: Summary Principles
sections.summary: Schmid summarizes with six principles: give trust but verify, stop fighting the model by forcing rigid workflows, preserve meaning as context, design for recovery since agents are imperfect, evaluate rather than only assert, and build to delete because the bitter lesson means software is disposable and will be rebuilt with better models. He points to his blog for deeper code examples.

demonstrations: Deep research agent returning a plan that users can approve while adding natural-language constraints like 'focus on US market, ignore California'
Temperature preference example: user from Europe normally using Celsius but wanting Fahrenheit for cooking, which flags cannot dynamically capture
Subscription cancellation flow where agent dynamically reacts to changing user intent rather than following a fixed workflow
deleteItem endpoint as example of an API that feels self-explanatory to its developer but is opaque to an agent seeing only the schema and docstring
limitations: Agents are non-deterministic and cannot guarantee the same input always produces the same output
Agents are not 100% reliable, especially over longer running times where unexpected things happen
Traditional Boolean flags and data structures cannot capture dynamic user preferences or semantic meaning
quantitativeClaims: Agent runs can take 5 to 15 minutes, making restart-from-scratch costly
A customer agent that only works 1 out of 10 times is not production-ready
